claim: Only 59.8 percent of US artists worked full-year and full-time versus 66.0 percent of all US workers, and for the performing occupations closest to content creation the share collapses to 23.5 percent for actors, 32.6 percent for musicians and 37.5 percent for entertainers.
stance_target: The position that creative occupations sustain full-time work at far lower rates than the general workforce, so headline creative earnings describe a minority who survived
scope_conditions: United States only; American Community Survey PUMS 2015-2019, more than 119,000 artists unweighted; nationally representative; pre-COVID; full-year/full-time defined as 50+ weeks at 35+ hours; occupation-based, not platform-based
quoted_support: Fewer than 60 percent of artists worked "full-year, full time" (defined as working 50-52 weeks for at least 35 hours per week). This compared with 66 percent of all U.S. workers.

claim: Median annual earnings of US artists working full-year and full-time were $58,005 in 2015-2019, about $10,000 above the $48,305 median for all US workers, but this figure is conditioned on full-time survival and therefore excludes the 40 percent of artists who did not achieve it.
stance_target: The claim that creative occupations are inherently low-paid, and simultaneously the claim that reported creative-occupation medians describe typical creative earners
scope_conditions: United States only; ACS PUMS 2015-2019, more than 119,000 artists unweighted; restricted to full-year/full-time workers with $1 or more in earnings; constant dollars; excludes part-year and part-time artists entirely
quoted_support: the median annual earnings of full-year, full-time artists in 2015-2019 were $58,005, about $10,000 greater than for all workers ($48,305).

claim: US artists are self-employed at 33.6 percent versus 9.3 percent for the entire US labour force, and above 45 percent for photographers, fine artists, entertainers and musicians, which is why payroll-based statistics systematically miss most creative earners.
stance_target: The position that administrative payroll data undercounts creative and creator workers, making household surveys the only viable administrative source
scope_conditions: United States only; ACS PUMS 2015-2019; self-employment measured as primary-job status
quoted_support: nearly 34 percent of artists were self-employed, compared with just over 9 percent of all workers.

claim: The US artist workforce numbered 2.4 million people across 11 occupations, of whom 247,570 were writers and authors, 216,065 musicians, 190,154 photographers and 171,273 producers and directors.
stance_target: The size of the administratively-measured creative occupational workforce in the United States
scope_conditions: United States only; ACS PUMS 2015-2019; workers classified by primary job in hours worked, so anyone whose creative work is secondary is excluded from these counts
quoted_support: In 2015-2019, the U.S. workforce contained 2.4 million artists--defined as workers whose primary job (in terms of number of hours worked on a given week) fell into one of 11 distinct occupations.

claim: Women artists working full-year and full-time earned $0.80 for every dollar earned by men artists, exactly matching the economy-wide ratio, so creative work confers no gender-equity advantage in the United States.
stance_target: The claim that creative and independent work reduces gendered earnings inequality
scope_conditions: United States only; ACS PUMS 2015-2019; full-year/full-time workers with $1 or more in earnings; ratios computed on unrounded data; dancers/choreographers suppressed for small sample
quoted_support: In 2015-2019, women artists (working full-year, full-time) earned $0.80 for every dollar earned by men artists; the same ratio is reported for all women workers in the labor force
